# Summary

Only a small share of clients contacted through phone sales agree to subscribe to a term deposit: in our data, about 12% of contacted clients subscribed. Because every call costs the bank money and staff time, this makes phone marketing costly. In this project we aim to improve the efficiency of this type of marketing by asking whether information available before a call (a client's demographic characteristics, financial health and the outcome of the previous campaign) can predict whether the client will subscribe. We trained a logistic regression model on the UCI Bank Marketing dataset (Moro, Rita, et al., 2014). On the test set, the model had an F1 of 0.3507 and correctly identified 472 of the 1,058 actual subscribers. These results suggest that pre-call information carries some useful signal, but at the tuned 0.15 classification threshold the model still missed most subscribers. The model also assumes linear relationships, which may miss patterns such as the U-shaped relationship between age and subscription, and it was evaluated on a single test split, so its performance in future campaigns may differ.

# Introduction

A term deposit is a savings product in which a client places money with a bank for a fixed period in exchange for a fixed interest rate. The Bank Marketing dataset records direct marketing campaigns in which a Portuguese bank promoted term deposits to its clients through phone calls, often contacting the same client more than once (Moro et al., 2011; Moro, Rita, et al., 2014). In this data, only about 12% of contacted clients subscribed.

This low success rate makes mass calling inefficient. Every unsuccessful call costs the bank money and uses staff time that could be spent on clients who are more likely to be interested. Repeated calls to clients who do not want the product can also frustrate them and harm customer satisfaction. And missing customers who are likely to accept costs the bank profits. Predicting which clients are likely to accept a term deposit would allow the bank to better match clients with the banking products they need, increasing client satisfaction, financial security and banking profits. Previous work on this dataset has shown that data mining models can help predict the success of bank telemarketing calls (Moro et al., 2011; Moro, Cortez, et al., 2014).

In this project we ask: **can a client's demographic characteristics, financial health and previous campaign outcome, all known before a marketing call, be used to predict whether the client will subscribe to a term deposit, so that the bank can target likely subscribers instead of mass calling?** We focus only on information known before the call, rather than details of the call itself such as its duration, because the bank needs to decide whom to call before making the call.

# Methods

## Data

We used the Bank Marketing dataset created by Moro, Rita, et al. (2014) and made available through the UCI Machine Learning Repository under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 (CC BY 4.0) license. The data comes from phone-based direct marketing campaigns run by a Portuguese bank between May 2008 and November 2010 (Moro et al., 2011). We used the full version of the data, which contains 45,211 rows. Each row represents one client contacted during a campaign and includes 16 explanatory variables and a binary target recording whether the client subscribed to a term deposit ("yes" or "no"). The dataset has no blank missing values. Unknown values are instead recorded as an "unknown" category, which we kept as its own level (Moro, Rita, et al., 2014).

We divided the explanatory variables used in this analysis into three groups, shown in @tbl-variables. We did not use the remaining seven variables. Most of them describe the contact made during the current campaign, such as the call duration, which is only known after the call has taken place.

| Group | Variables |
|----------------------------|--------------------------------------------|
| Demographic | Age (years), marital status (married, single or divorced, where divorced also includes widowed), job type, education level |
| Financial health | Credit default, average yearly account balance (euros), housing loan, personal loan |
| Previous decision | Outcome of the previous marketing campaign (success, failure, other or unknown) |

: Explanatory variables used in this analysis, grouped by type. {#tbl-variables}

```{r}
# Downloading raw data
# The download is skipped if the file is already present, so re-knitting doesn't
# hit the server each time.
data_url <- "https://archive.ics.uci.edu/static/public/222/bank+marketing.zip"
raw_dir  <- file.path("..", "data", "raw")
dir.create(raw_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

zip_path <- file.path(raw_dir, "bank+marketing.zip")

if (!file.exists(zip_path)) {
  options(timeout = max(300, getOption("timeout")))   # slow connections
  download.file(data_url, destfile = zip_path, mode = "wb")
}

# Unzip the outer archive, then the inner bank.zip (skipped if already extracted)
if (!file.exists(file.path(raw_dir, "bank-full.csv"))) {
  unzip(zip_path, exdir = raw_dir)
  inner_zip <- file.path(raw_dir, "bank.zip")
  if (file.exists(inner_zip)) unzip(inner_zip, exdir = raw_dir)
}

raw_csv <- list.files(raw_dir, pattern = "^bank-full\\.csv$",
                      recursive = TRUE, full.names = TRUE)[1]
stopifnot("bank-full.csv not found after unzipping" = !is.na(raw_csv))

raw_csv
list.files(raw_dir, recursive = TRUE)

bank_raw <- read_delim(raw_csv, delim = ";", show_col_types = FALSE)
month_levels <- c("jan", "feb", "mar", "apr", "may", "jun",
                  "jul", "aug", "sep", "oct", "nov", "dec")

# Cleaning the data
bank_clean <- bank_raw |>
  mutate(
    across(where(is.character), as.factor),
    y      = factor(y, levels = c("no", "yes")),
    month  = factor(month, levels = month_levels)
  ) 

# Sanity checks
stopifnot(nrow(bank_clean) == nrow(bank_raw),
          !anyNA(bank_clean$y),
          all(!is.na(bank_clean$month)))

# Saving cleaned data
processed_dir <- file.path("...", "data", "processed")
dir.create(processed_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

write_csv(bank_clean, file.path(processed_dir, "bank_clean.csv"))
```

## Analysis

We used logistic regression to predict whether a client would subscribe to a term deposit. The outcome is binary, and logistic regression estimates a subscription probability for each client. These probabilities allow the bank to rank clients for outreach, while the model coefficients help explain how each predictor is associated with subscription when the other predictors are held fixed. Because only a small proportion of clients subscribed, the default classification threshold of 0.50 can miss many actual subscribers. Lowering the threshold can identify more subscribers, but it can also flag more clients who do not subscribe. We therefore used stratified five-fold cross-validation on the training set to examine how different thresholds affect precision, recall, and F1. We chose our threshold with F1 being the classification metric, as the goal is determining clients who might buy the term deposits and missing clients who would buy and calling many who won't is bad for the banks profits and resource allocation.

Before any exploration or modelling, the data was split into a training set (80%, 36,168 clients) and a test set (20%, 9,043 clients), so that the test set did not influence any of our decisions. The analysis was carried out in R (R Core Team, 2026) using the tidyverse (Wickham et al., 2019) for data wrangling and visualization and tidymodels (Kuhn & Wickham, 2020) for modelling. All variables were standardized just prior to model fitting.

```{r}
# Creating splits
bank_split <- initial_split(bank_clean, prop = 0.8, strata = y) 
bank_train <- training(bank_split) 
bank_test <- testing(bank_split)

write_csv(bank_train, file.path(processed_dir, "bank_train.csv")) 
write_csv(bank_test, file.path(processed_dir, "bank_test.csv"))

tibble(set = c("train", "test"), 
       n = c(nrow(bank_train), nrow(bank_test)), 
       yes_rate = c(mean(bank_train$y == "yes"), mean(bank_test$y == "yes")))
```

### Summary of exploratory findings

Among the demographic variables, age and job showed the largest differences in subscription rate. Subscription followed a U-shaped pattern by age, being highest for the youngest and oldest clients, while education and marital status showed smaller differences. Among the financial health variables, having a housing loan, a personal loan or a credit default was associated with lower subscription, and a higher account balance was associated with slightly higher subscription. Because the target is imbalanced, with about 12% of clients subscribing, we evaluated models using recall as well as accuracy.

## Preprocessing

We used nine predictors available before the current marketing call: age, marital status, occupation, education, credit default, average yearly account balance, housing loan status, personal loan status, and the outcome of the previous marketing campaign. We kept the existing training and test split and treated subscription as the positive class.

We converted categorical predictors to indicator variables and standardized age and account balance. During cross-validation, we estimated these transformations using only the training portion of each fold and applied them to that fold’s validation data. For the final evaluation, we estimated the transformations on the full training set and applied them to the test set.

## Training-set evaluation

We chose to use a classification model using a Logistic Regression with all nine predictors. To predict whether a client would accept the term deposit, We compared ten classification thresholds using stratified five-fold cross-validation and checked across a range of possible thresholds below 0.5 due to the heavily imbalanced classes in our dataset. We found that a threshold of 0.15 was optimal among the thresholds tested due to having the highest mean F1 score. Because the threshold was selected using only training-data folds, the test set gives an unbiased estimate of performance.

```{r}
#| include: false
# Read in training data
train_df <- read_csv("../data/processed/bank_train.csv")

training_data <- train_df|>
  select(age, marital, job, education, default, balance, housing, loan, poutcome, y)|>
  mutate(y = factor(y, levels = c("yes","no")))

predictor_cols <- c(
  "age", "marital", "job", "education", "default", "balance",
  "housing", "loan", "poutcome")
model_cols <- c(predictor_cols, "y")

# preprocessor
preprocessor <- recipe(y ~ ., data = training_data) |>
  step_dummy(marital, job, education, default, housing, loan, poutcome) |>
  step_normalize(age, balance)

# logistic regression
logistic_model <- logistic_reg() |>
  set_engine("glm") |>
  set_mode("classification")

pipe_logistic <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(preprocessor) |>
  add_model(logistic_model)

# 5-fold cross validation
folds <- vfold_cv(training_data, v = 5, strata = y)
cv_metrics <- metric_set(accuracy, recall, precision, f_meas, roc_auc)

logistic_cv <- fit_resamples(
  pipe_logistic,
  resamples = folds,
  metrics = cv_metrics,
  control = control_resamples(save_pred = TRUE))

preds <- collect_predictions(logistic_cv)
thresholds <- seq(0.05, 0.50, by = 0.05)

# Precision, recall, and F1 at each threshold
multi_metrics <- metric_set(f_meas, precision, recall, accuracy)

threshold_full <- map(thresholds, \(t) {
  preds |>
    mutate(.pred_class = factor(if_else(.pred_yes >= t, "yes", "no"),
                                levels = c("yes", "no"))) |>
    group_by(id) |>
    multi_metrics(truth = y, estimate = .pred_class) |>
    group_by(.metric) |>
    summarise(mean = mean(.estimate, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
    mutate(threshold = t)
}) |>
  list_rbind()
```

@tbl-bank-thresholds compares the mean F1, precision, recall, and accuracy across the five cross-validation folds for each candidate threshold.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-bank-thresholds
#| tbl-cap: "Mean cross-validation scores for the ten candidate classification thresholds, ranked by F1."
#| echo: false

threshold_full |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = .metric, values_from = mean) |>
  arrange(desc(f_meas)) |>
  select(Threshold = threshold,
         `F1 (%)` = f_meas,
         `Precision (%)` = precision,
         `Recall (%)` = recall,
         `Accuracy (%)` = accuracy) |>
  mutate(across(-Threshold, \(x) 100 * x)) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2, align = "c")
```

## Test-set evaluation

We refitted the logistic regression model on the full training set and evaluated it on the original test set. We classified clients as predicted subscribers when their estimated probability was at least 0.15. We report accuracy for overall classification performance, precision for the share of predicted subscribers who actually subscribed, and recall for the share of actual subscribers the model identified. The F1 score summarizes precision and recall.

```{r}
# Test data evaluation
test_data <- read_csv("../data/processed/bank_test.csv")
# Predict on test data
logistic_fit <- fit(pipe_logistic, data = training_data)

# Adjust the threshold to 0.15
logistic_prob <- predict(logistic_fit, test_data, type = "prob")$.pred_yes
actual_yes <- test_data$y == "yes"
logistic_yes <- logistic_prob >= 0.15

accuracy = mean(logistic_yes == actual_yes)
precision = mean(actual_yes[logistic_yes])
recall = mean(logistic_yes[actual_yes])

# Calculate F1 and other metric scores
scores <- rbind(
  "Logistic regression" = c(
    accuracy = accuracy,
    precision = precision,
    recall = recall,
    f1 = 2 * precision * recall / (precision + recall)
  )
)
```

@tbl-bank-test summarizes the test-set accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 score at the 0.15 classification threshold.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-bank-test
#| tbl-cap: "Test-set accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 for logistic regression at the 0.15 classification threshold."
#| echo: false

kable(data.frame(
  Model = rownames(scores),
  F1 = sprintf("%.2f%%", 100 * scores[, "f1"]),
  Precision = sprintf("%.2f%%", 100 * scores[, "precision"]),
  Recall = sprintf("%.2f%%", 100 * scores[, "recall"]),
  Accuracy = sprintf("%.2f%%", 100 * scores[, "accuracy"]),
  check.names = FALSE,
  row.names = NULL
))
```

Test performance was consistent with cross-validation (F1 35.07% vs. 35.56%), suggesting the model did not overfit (@tbl-bank-thresholds and @tbl-bank-test). However, the model is still miscategorizing many clients. The confusion matrix shows that the model has more false negatives than true positives. A false negative means a likely subscriber is never called, so the bank loses a sale and the client misses a product that suited them.Additionally, the model also has a large number of false positives, which may be harmful to the bank if resources are scarce and efficient allocation is needed.

```{r}
test_preds_class <- tibble(
  y = factor(test_data$y, levels = c("yes", "no")),
  .pred_class = factor(if_else(logistic_prob >= 0.15, "yes", "no"),
                       levels = c("yes", "no"))
)

cm_test <- conf_mat(test_preds_class, truth = y, estimate = .pred_class)
cm_test
#autoplot(cm_test, type = "heatmap") 
```

While there is promise in this model as a tool to build a more targeted call list to match clients with term deposits, it still requires more work. The logistic regression model did show that information available before a marketing call can help identify clients who are likely to subscribe to a term deposit. However, even using a threshold of 0.15 to maximize the F1 score, recall was only 44.61%, meaning the model still missed 55.39% of the clients who would have invested in term deposits. While tuning on a slightly finer grid may help to improve our score metrics, it is likely our predictor variables may not be carrying a strong enough signal. Logistic regression assumes that age and account balance have linear relationships with the log-odds of subscription and that predictor effects are additive on the log-odds scale. These assumptions may miss nonlinear patterns or interactions among client characteristics.

Additionally, we evaluated the model on one test split, so its performance may differ in later campaigns. The data source (Moro et al., 2014) is also limited to Portugeuse banking clients from the period of 2008-2013. This specific time and location sample, which includes the 2008 Financial Crisis, may affect applicability to other countries and/or time periods.

A follow-up study could evaluate the model on a later campaign and ask how many subscribers it identifies when the bank can contact only a fixed number of clients.

# Results

As shown in @fig-bank-test-metrics, logistic regression achieved 80.67% accuracy and an F1 score of 35.07% on the test set at the 0.15 classification threshold. The model identified 472 of the 1,058 clients who subscribed, yielding a recall of 44.61%. Of the 1,634 clients predicted to subscribe, 472 actually did, yielding a precision of 28.89%.

```{r}
#| label: fig-bank-test-metrics
#| fig-cap: "Test-set accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 for logistic regression at the 0.15 classification threshold."
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 3.5
#| echo: false

metric_plot_data <- data.frame(
  metric = factor(
    c("Accuracy", "Precision", "Recall", "F1"),
    levels = rev(c("Accuracy", "Precision", "Recall", "F1"))
  ),
  percent = 100 * unname(scores["Logistic regression", c("accuracy", "precision", "recall", "f1")])
)

ggplot(metric_plot_data, aes(x = percent, y = metric)) +
  geom_col(fill = "blue", width = 0.5) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = sprintf("%.2f%%", percent)),
    hjust = 0,
    size = 4
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = seq(0, 100, by = 20),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.02))
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 100)) +
  labs(x = "Test-set score (%)", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

The confusion matrix in @fig-bank-test-confusion shows how the errors were distributed. The model missed 586 actual subscribers and incorrectly predicted subscription for 1,162 non-subscribers. It correctly classified 6,823 of the 7,985 non-subscribers. Overall, the model correctly identified a substantially larger share of non-subscribers than subscribers.

```{r}
#| label: fig-bank-test-confusion
#| fig-cap: "Test-set confusion matrix for logistic regression at the 0.15 classification threshold. Rows show predicted outcomes and columns show actual outcomes."
#| echo: false

autoplot(cm_test, type = "heatmap")
```

At the 0.15 threshold, the model flagged 1,634 of the 9,043 test-set clients (18.1%). This group contained 44.6% of all actual subscribers. The observed subscription rate among flagged clients was 28.89%, about 2.5 times the overall test-set rate of 11.70%. Thus, actual subscribers were more concentrated in the group flagged by the model.

Our results suggest that information available before a marketing call can help identify clients who are likely to subscribe to a term deposit. At the classification threshold of 0.15, logistic regression achieved an F1 score of 35.07%, with 28.89% precision, 44.61% recall, and 80.67% accuracy on the test set. The model identified 472 of the 1,058 actual subscribers and missed 586. We expected accuracy to give an incomplete picture because most clients did not subscribe. Recall shows how many subscribers the model found, while precision shows how many clients on its proposed call list ultimately subscribed.

The model flagged 1,634 clients for outreach, which 1,162 of them did not subscribe. In practical terms, about 29 out of every 100 clients on the proposed list subscribed. This illustrates the decision the bank faces. A longer call list may reach more potential subscribers, but it also takes more time and increases the number of calls to clients who do not subscribe. The value of the model therefore depends on the bank's call budget and the value of reaching additional subscribers.

Prasad et al. (2025) compared several classifiers for the same prediction task. Their blending model had the highest reported accuracy in their comparison (90.5%), with 74.59% precision and 23.62% recall. Our logistic regression had higher observed recall and lower observed precision. These figures provide context for the different priorities a bank might have when building a call list. The studies used different data and predictors, so a direct model comparison would require evaluating both approaches on the same test set with the same pre-call information.

Logistic regression assumes that the effects of predictors are additive on the log-odds scale and that age and account balance enter as linear terms on that scale. This may limit its ability to capture patterns such as the U-shaped relationship between age and subscription rate observed in the training data. We also evaluated the model on a single test split, so performance may differ in later campaigns. Overall, logistic regression provides a starting point for prioritizing outreach, although it still misses more than half of actual subscribers. A follow-up study could compare logistic regression with a model on a later campaign and measure how many subscribers each model identifies under the same call budget.
